changes: case prompts: revised per-type strategy (cheap branch closers for case, one general key for have), plus a route cue when the original proof does `induction x` and unfolds a function the statement applies to x, the locations of repeated blocks, and an objective sentence (make_prompts.py).

case_prompts.P01: This proof is mainly `case` branches (97.4% of proof tokens). Branches: separately written branches often repeat the same steps. Before editing branches one by one, check whether several branches reach the same remaining goal after one normalization step, and whether a different way of splitting the cases lets one shared rule close them together. Keep a branch separate only if it needs its own argument. After choosing the split, close each branch with the cheapest step that works (`rfl`, `assumption`, `exact ..`, `simp only [..]`) before a broad `simp_all` or `grind` over all hypotheses: one blanket closer is short but can cost many heartbeats. Route menu for this problem, in order: (1) split along the definition of `substOld` (for example `fun_induction substOld ...`), since the original splits with `induction post` and then unfolds `substOld`; (2) no induction: build the goal directly from lemmas in the context about the predicates and functions in the statement, as one chain of `refine`/`exact`/`rw`; (3) keep the original split; merge branches that end the same way and close them cheaply. Compile at least one complete candidate on each of the first two routes before polishing one. If three candidates in a row do not lower the objective, switch to the next route in the menu instead of polishing further. Judge every rewrite by the objective in the common instructions, which adds the token ratio and the heartbeat ratio: the shortest proof is not always the best. A helper lemma or a broad automation call is worth it only if what it saves in one ratio outweighs what it adds in the other.
